questions.question: What is the primary root cause of the memory leak in this implementation?
options: A) The `@Transactional` annotation creates a CGLIB proxy that captures and prevents GC collection of the `OrderProcessingService` instance.
B) Pooled worker threads from `fixedThreadPoolTaskExecutor` retain strong references to `AUDIT_CONTEXT`'s map values within their `ThreadLocalMap`, and `remove()` is never invoked.
C) The `ThreadLocal` key is a weak reference in `ThreadLocalMap`, causing the GC to reclaim the key on minor collections and nullify the map reference.
D) `CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null)` prevents the Spring `@Async` proxy from triggering default transaction synchronization cleanups.
questions.correct_answer_text: B) Pooled worker threads from `fixedThreadPoolTaskExecutor` retain strong references to `AUDIT_CONTEXT`'s map values within their `ThreadLocalMap`, and `remove()` is never invoked.
questions.explanation: In Java, `ThreadLocal` stores entries in each `Thread`'s internal `ThreadLocalMap`. Because worker threads in `fixedThreadPoolTaskExecutor` are pooled and kept alive indefinitely, any state associated with the thread persists across tasks. Furthermore, because `AUDIT_CONTEXT` is a `static final` reference, the key itself is strongly referenced, keeping the `Entry` and its large `payload` strongly reachable in the Old Generation. Failing to call `AUDIT_CONTEXT.remove()` in a `finally` block guarantees that every pooled thread retains heavy allocations indefinitely.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where an ultra-high-throughput payment orchestration service deployed with G1GC (`-XX:+UseG1GC`) on a 32GB heap experiences sudden latency spikes of 700ms+. The GC logs highlight frequent occurrences of `to-space exhausted` (also known as evacuation failure) during Young GC cycles, rapidly followed by a Full GC cycle.
questions.question: What is the primary mechanism causing this evacuation failure, and which JVM tuning strategy is the most appropriate remedy?
options: A) Surviving objects could not fit into the available survivor or free regions during a pause; increase `-XX:G1ReservePercent` and lower `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` (IHOP).
B) The Young generation generation size exceeded `-XX:NewRatio`; decrease `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` to force more aggressive concurrent cycles.
C) The JVM metaspace ran out of space during proxy reflection; increase `-XX:MetaspaceSize` and enable `-XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent`.
D) Tenured objects failed string deduplication passes; disable `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication` to reclaim thread headroom.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) Surviving objects could not fit into the available survivor or free regions during a pause; increase `-XX:G1ReservePercent` and lower `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` (IHOP).
questions.explanation: In G1GC, an evacuation failure (`to-space exhausted`) happens when G1 attempts to evacuate (copy) live objects from Eden/Survivor regions into Survivor or Old regions, but finds no free regions available. This triggers expensive in-place object pinning and frequently cascades into an un-parallelized or slow Full GC. The standard remediations are: (1) Increasing `-XX:G1ReservePercent` (default is 10%) to preserve a larger buffer of empty regions for surviving objects, and (2) Lowering `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` (IHOP) so that the concurrent marking cycle initiates earlier before Old Gen fills up.

questions.scenario: You are debugging a production issue where a long-running Spring Boot service experiences gradual native memory expansion, eventually throwing `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` after several weeks. Heap inspection reveals stable Tenured and Eden utilization. Thread dumps and heap dumps reveal thousands of classes named `com.example.service.ReportService$$SpringCGLIB$$FastClass$$...` and `...EnhancerBySpringCGLIB$$...` continuously being defined.
questions.question: Which of the following architectural bugs is the most likely cause of this continuous class creation?
options: A) A custom interceptor repeatedly creates new `org.springframework.aop.framework.ProxyFactory` instances at runtime per request without caching, forcing dynamic CGLIB byte generation.
B) The service contains `@Transactional` methods marked with `propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW`, forcing new CGLIB wrappers on each transaction invocation.
C) The JVM's tiered compilation is failing to deoptimize cold methods, causing compiled classes to leak from the CodeCache into Metaspace.
D) Spring context re-creates scoped beans because `@RequestScope` beans cannot be collected until the application server halts.
questions.correct_answer_text: A) A custom interceptor repeatedly creates new `org.springframework.aop.framework.ProxyFactory` instances at runtime per request without caching, forcing dynamic CGLIB byte generation.
questions.explanation: Standard Spring proxying (such as via `@Transactional` or `@Service` annotations) creates dynamic proxy classes once during bean post-processing at application startup and caches them. However, if custom logic dynamically creates new `ProxyFactory` or `org.springframework.cglib.proxy.Enhancer` instances per incoming request (or fails to configure CGLIB class caching via `Enhancer.setUseCache(true)`), new bytecode and class metadata are generated and loaded into a ClassLoader for every invocation. Because class metadata resides in Metaspace and dynamic classes with non-collectible ClassLoaders cannot be unloaded, Metaspace will experience an irreversible memory leak.
